headline: Training, leadership and the right to practice
summary: Black nurses built training schools, cared for communities, won professional recognition and challenged unequal treatment at work. These records name the people, institutions and decisions behind those changes—and distinguish education from hiring, promotion and equal working conditions.
coverageNote: Thirteen selected episodes across hospital training, community care, university leadership, military nursing and employment rights. Named workplaces include Provident in Chicago, Florida A&M, NYU, Freedmen’s/Howard, Dixie Hospital and Kaiser’s Oakland Medical Center. These are distinct histories, not a proven chain to every nursing job.
question: Which admission, appointment or employment record connects this history to your nursing workplace?

events.title: Mary Eliza Mahoney completes formal nurse training
events.decisionMaker: New England Hospital for Women and Children Training School for Nurses
events.barrier: Mahoney had to complete the hospital school’s demanding 16-month course.
events.change: She graduated in 1879; the American Nurses Association identifies her as America’s first Black professional nurse.
events.outcome: She worked as a nurse and later welcomed the first National Association of Colored Graduate Nurses conference in 1909.
events.limit: This record establishes a training credential and professional participation, not a modern state RN license or nationwide access to hospital jobs.

source.title: American Nurses Association · Mary Eliza Mahoney
source.locator: Mary Eliza Mahoney biography, graduation and 1909 conference paragraphs
source.supports: Mahoney’s 1879 graduation, the training institution and course length, and her 1909 conference address.

events.title: Emma Reynolds’ exclusion helps spur a new nursing school
events.people: Emma Reynolds, Reverend Louis Reynolds and Daniel Hale Williams
events.decisionMaker: Williams and Provident’s organizers established a hospital and nurse training school in Chicago
events.barrier: Chicago nursing schools denied Reynolds admission because she was Black.
events.change: After efforts to win her admission elsewhere failed, the organizers founded Provident Hospital and its training school in 1891.
events.outcome: Reynolds graduated from Provident’s early nursing class. Training capacity grew through an institution built in response to exclusion.
events.limit: This is Chicago’s Provident, not another hospital with the same name. It closed in 1987 and reopened under Cook County in 1993; a current job needs its own appointment record.

source.title: Chicago History Museum · Provident Hospital
source.locator: Brittany Hutchinson, July 29, 2020; paragraphs on Emma Reynolds, founding and the first graduating class
source.supports: Reynolds’ exclusion, the founders’ response and her graduation from the new school.

sources.title: Cook County Health · Provident’s 30th anniversary timeline
sources.supports: The founding context, closure and later county reopening; not continuous employment since 1891.

events.title: Jessie Sleet Scales takes nursing into Black households
events.decisionMaker: New York’s Charity Organization Society employed Scales for community nursing
events.barrier: Black residents faced obstacles to hospital care and tuberculosis treatment; nursing work also faced racial restrictions.
events.change: Scales began district nursing in 1900. The work connected home visits and practical health education with treatment for tuberculosis.
events.outcome: A 1901 nursing-journal account records this work. Her reports also connected people’s health with housing and employment discrimination.
events.limit: This was work for a private social-service organization in New York City. It is not proof of a city-government appointment, a modern RN license or a current home-care agency’s hiring route.

source.title: University of Rochester · A history of care exhibit
source.locator: Item headed Jessie Sleet Scales, “A Successful Experiment,” American Journal of Nursing 1(10), 1901, pp. 729–31
source.supports: The 1900 district-nursing appointment, tuberculosis work and an exhibited contemporary account.

sources.title: University of Illinois Chicago · Black public health nurses
sources.locator: “Black public health nurses: skills & impact,” final paragraph on Scales and the Charity Organization Society; indexed page text
sources.supports: Identifies her private employer and reports connecting home conditions and employment discrimination to health.

events.title: Martha Minerva Franklin turns exclusion into collective organizing
events.people: Martha Minerva Franklin and the founding nurses of NACGN
events.decisionMaker: Nurses meeting in New York formed the National Association of Colored Graduate Nurses and elected Franklin president
events.barrier: Black nurses faced discrimination in professional opportunities and needed an organization able to act on their conditions.
events.change: Franklin gathered information from Black nurses and called the founding meeting, sponsored by the Lincoln School for Nurses Alumnae Association.
events.outcome: The new association set goals for professional standards, leadership and ending discrimination. Its surviving records describe later campaigns for jobs and military service.
events.limit: Organizing created a vehicle for change; founding an association did not itself change a hospital’s hiring policy. The catalog description was reviewed, not the underlying meeting minutes.

source.title: NYPL Schomburg Center · NACGN records
source.locator: Biographical/historical information, opening paragraph; indexed finding aid, collection Sc Micro R 6565
source.supports: Franklin’s survey, the sponsoring alumnae association, the 1908 founding and its stated goals.

events.title: Staupers and Black nurses press for military admission
events.people: Mabel Keaton Staupers and the National Association of Colored Graduate Nurses
events.decisionMaker: Army and Navy nursing authorities; Staupers and NACGN advocated for the change
events.barrier: Qualified Black nurses faced racial restrictions on military nursing service during World War II.
events.change: Staupers organized a letter-writing campaign, met Eleanor Roosevelt and pressed officials to use Black nurses’ skills.
events.outcome: The National Park Service account dates the military’s acceptance of qualified nurses regardless of race to 1945.
events.limit: This institutional history describes an admission change; it does not establish equal assignments, promotion or the service record of an individual nurse.

source.title: National Park Service · Places of Mabel Keaton Staupers
source.locator: Opening biography and section 3, Eleanor Roosevelt’s Apartment
source.supports: Staupers’ organizing, contact with Eleanor Roosevelt and the account’s 1945 military admission change.

events.title: Mary Elizabeth Carnegie strengthens nursing education at Florida A&M
events.people: Mary Elizabeth Carnegie and Florida A&M’s nursing faculty and students
events.decisionMaker: Carnegie led the program; college administrators authorized its separate educational responsibilities and budget
events.barrier: Nursing education operated within the hospital’s administration, limiting faculty control over students’ preparation.
events.change: As dean, Carnegie reorganized faculty, secured a separate budget and strengthened clinical instruction. She also shortened students’ duty hours and improved textbooks and records.
events.outcome: Nursing became a college division responsible for its curriculum and clinical arrangements, separating educational oversight from hospital service needs.
events.limit: These are documented educational and administrative changes during her 1945–1953 tenure. They do not establish each graduate’s license, later employer or measured patient outcomes.

source.title: University of Virginia · Carnegie’s educational leadership
source.locator: Windows in Time, Spring 2021, printed pages 14–15; Carnegie’s Florida A&M reforms
source.supports: The reorganization, budget, teaching resources, student duty hours and move to college oversight.

sources.title: Nurses Educational Funds · Mary Elizabeth Carnegie
sources.locator: Memorial biography; paragraph recording her Florida A&M deanship, 1945–1953
sources.supports: The dates and institutional location of her deanship.

events.title: Estelle Massey Osborne joins NYU’s nursing faculty
events.decisionMaker: New York University appointed Osborne; the reviewed accounts do not identify the appointing official
events.barrier: Advanced nursing education and faculty positions were separate barriers for Black nurses.
events.change: After earning a nursing master’s at Teachers College in 1931, Osborne became NYU’s first Black nursing faculty member, according to NYU’s institutional account.
events.outcome: NYU describes eight years of teaching and mentoring Black students and nurses—a specific appointment and sustained work, not only an honorary recognition.
events.limit: NYU’s account dates her arrival to 1946; NYPL’s finding aid says 1947. An appointment record is still needed to resolve that difference. This faculty role does not establish employment at an NYU hospital.

source.title: NYU Meyers · Estelle Osborne’s legacy
source.locator: 2017 legacy celebration account; paragraphs on the 1931 master’s and 1946 faculty appointment
source.supports: Her degree, NYU’s first-Black-faculty identification, its 1946 date and the mentoring described.

sources.title: NYPL Schomburg Center · Estelle Massey Osborne papers
sources.locator: Creator History, printed page ii (PDF page 2), paragraph recording a 1947 NYU appointment
sources.supports: An independent institutional account of the appointment with a conflicting year; underlying papers were not reviewed.

events.title: Black nurses gain full ANA membership
events.people: Mabel Keaton Staupers and Black nurses organizing through NACGN
events.decisionMaker: American Nurses Association; the biography does not identify the specific voting body
events.barrier: ANA membership had been denied to Black nurses living in some states.
events.change: Following years of organizing, Black nurses were admitted to full ANA membership in 1948.
events.outcome: The professional association’s membership barrier changed; ANA’s own biography records this result.
events.limit: Association membership is distinct from a nursing license, an employer’s hiring decision and equal treatment on the job.

source.title: American Nurses Association · Mabel Keaton Staupers
source.locator: Mabel Keaton Staupers biography, membership restrictions and 1948 admission
source.supports: The state-based membership exclusions and the 1948 admission of Black nurses to full ANA membership.

events.title: Congress protects eligible staff during the Howard transfer
events.people: Freedmen’s Hospital employees facing a change of employer
events.decisionMaker: U.S. Congress, with transfer terms to be agreed by the HEW secretary and Howard’s trustees
events.barrier: Transferring a federal hospital to a university put employees’ jobs, pay and benefits under a new employer.
events.change: Public Law 87-262 required transfer opportunities for eligible staff and prohibited salary reductions for covered employees who transferred.
events.outcome: The law also protected specified retirement, insurance and seniority arrangements.
events.limit: The protections applied to defined employee categories, not every applicant or later hire; this statute alone does not verify an individual worker’s transfer or payroll.

source.title: Public Law 87-262 · Transfer of Freedmen’s Hospital
source.supports: The transfer authority, eligible employee categories, salary protection and specified benefit and seniority provisions.

events.title: Three nurses win a ruling against discriminatory dismissal
events.people: Mildred M. Smith, Agnes L. Stokes and Patricia L. Taylor
events.decisionMaker: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit, with the opinion written by Judge Simon Sobeloff
events.barrier: Dixie Hospital in Hampton, Virginia, fired the three Black nurses—two practical nurses and one RN—after they ate in its white employees’ cafeteria.
events.change: They challenged their dismissal; the appeals court rejected the hospital’s defense and reversed the lower court.
events.outcome: The court directed reinstatement offers and recognized entitlement to back pay, reduced by interim earnings.
events.limit: The opinion establishes ordered relief at this hospital, not evidence that every remedy was carried out or that all nursing workplaces changed.

source.title: Smith v. Hampton Training School for Nurses · 360 F.2d 577
source.locator: Opinion: opening facts and final reinstatement/back-pay paragraphs
source.supports: The named nurses’ dismissal, their different nursing qualifications and the court’s reinstatement and back-pay directions.

events.title: Anna B. Coles leads Howard’s new nursing degree program
events.people: Anna B. Coles, founding dean, and Howard’s first BSN cohort
events.decisionMaker: Howard University Board of Trustees approved the program; Coles led the school
events.barrier: Freedmen’s hospital-based diploma training and a university bachelor’s program were different educational routes.
events.change: The trustees approved a baccalaureate nursing program on April 23, 1968; instruction began in 1969 under the new school’s leadership.
events.outcome: Howard’s first BSN cohort graduated in 1973, documenting an implemented degree program rather than only an announcement.
events.limit: This establishes Howard’s education pathway; graduation alone does not establish licensure or an appointment at Howard University Hospital or another employer.

source.title: Howard University · College of Nursing and Allied Health history
source.locator: History of the college, PDF page 8; Appendix A, PDF page 18
source.supports: Coles’ leadership and the nursing program’s development; the additional sources separate trustee approval from instruction and graduation.

sources.title: Howard University President · Nursing program approval
sources.supports: The April 23, 1968 trustee decision establishing the baccalaureate program; cited for that decision only.

sources.title: Howard University · BSN program’s 50th anniversary
sources.locator: September 16, 2019; paragraph beginning “The Bachelor of Science in Nursing program”; reproduced Coles account below
sources.supports: Instruction beginning in 1969, the first cohort’s 1973 graduation and an excerpt of Coles’ 1969 account.

events.title: Black nurses build a national voice from local workplaces
events.people: Lauranne Sams, Betty Smith Williams, Jessie Cunningham and Dorothy Williams
events.decisionMaker: Black nurse organizers founded NBNA and adopted its constitution and bylaws
events.barrier: A nursing credential did not by itself secure professional influence or advancement.
events.change: Sams and fellow nurses formed the National Black Nurses Association in Cleveland in 1971; its 1972 meeting established the organization’s governing structure.
events.outcome: Kaiser’s history records Cunningham’s OB-GYN work and supervisory appointment at Oakland Medical Center in the 1960s. Cunningham and Williams also organized community health screenings through their local Black nurses’ association.
events.limit: The records connect named nurses to Oakland and professional organizing. They do not identify who approved Cunningham’s promotion or prove a hiring pathway across every Kaiser facility.

source.title: National Black Nurses Association · Founding history
source.locator: Founding account; 1970 California organizing, 1971 Cleveland meeting and 1972 constitution/bylaws
source.supports: The named organizers, founding meeting and adoption of the governing structure.

sources.title: Kaiser Permanente · Jessie Cunningham’s nursing career
sources.locator: May 1, 2014; “A model student and mentor” and “Making connections with Black colleagues”
sources.supports: Cunningham’s Oakland nursing and supervision; Cunningham and Williams’ local organizing.

events.title: Hazel Johnson-Brown leads the Army Nurse Corps
events.decisionMaker: U.S. Army leadership appointed Johnson-Brown chief of the Army Nurse Corps
events.barrier: Johnson-Brown’s path began with rejection from a nursing school because she was Black; senior military leadership presented another level of access.
events.change: A Harlem Hospital School of Nursing graduate, she entered the Army in 1955 and became its nurse corps chief on September 1, 1979.
events.outcome: She became the U.S. military’s first Black woman general officer. During her tenure, Army nursing practice standards were published as an official Department of the Army pamphlet.
events.limit: The appointment and practice standards establish institutional leadership, not equal promotion outcomes for every Black nurse or a reader’s commission at a particular Army hospital.

source.title: U.S. Army Medical Department · Hazel W. Johnson
source.locator: Sixteenth Chief profile; tenure dates, education, commission and Army Nurse Corps standards paragraphs
source.supports: Her training, commission, chief appointment, general-officer first and publication of the practice standards.

sources.title: National Museum of the U.S. Army · Hazel Johnson-Brown
sources.locator: Biography; West Chester rejection, Harlem training and 1979 appointment paragraphs
sources.supports: The discrimination she encountered before training and her later Army leadership.

furtherResearch: Identify licensure, appointment and promotion records for the reader’s exact hospital, unit or community-care employer; education, employment and professional membership are different connections.
Read NACGN minutes and wartime correspondence to connect organizing to particular nursing-school admissions and military appointments.
Resolve the conflicting 1946 and 1947 dates for Osborne’s NYU appointment using university personnel or faculty records.
Check implementation of the Dixie Hospital judgment and the Freedmen’s employee-transfer protections using employment and court records.
Trace changes of building, operator and ownership before attaching an old hospital record to a modern health system.
Expand practical nursing, nurse anesthesia, nursing assistants and public-health pathways without treating their training or licenses as interchangeable.
